sources.source: KIP-939: Support Participation in 2PC (Apache Kafka wiki)

items.item: Kafka already has a 2PC implementation controlled by its own transaction coordinator; supporting an external transaction coordinator would let Kafka become a participant in a distributed transaction with other systems

at.step: Reveal: a stuck transaction defended against, a door opened wider

items.item: Fencing is strictly a rejection, never a merge — a zombie instance's writes don't queue up behind the new one, they're simply turned away, which the toy coordinator models as an outright rejected return value, not a delay.

at.step: Reveal: a restart fences, it never merges

items.item: read_committed is purely a consumer-side filtering rule, not a broker-side erasure — an aborted transaction's bytes occupy exactly the same disk space whether or not any read_committed consumer ever asks for them.

at.step: Reveal: filtered at read time, not erased at write time

items.item: Consume-transform-produce closes the second of the two crash windows named earlier in this chapter, the one idempotence alone never touched — this topic is specifically the mechanism that closes it, not a restatement of idempotence.

at.step: Reveal: the second crash window, closed inside Kafka

items.item: KIP-890 and KIP-939 solve two different problems that both happen to extend transactions: one defends against a transaction that never finishes, the other lets a transaction extend past Kafka's own boundary.

at.step: Reveal: a stuck transaction defended against, a door opened wider

items.item: A Kafka transaction's guarantee stops exactly at Kafka's own boundary — nothing about it makes a write to a database, file, or API atomic with anything, which is precisely why KIP-939 and the next topic exist.
The toy TinyCoordinator and TinyLog models are deliberately simplified standalone simulations, not a port of Kafka's real broker code, since no real Kafka broker runs in this sandbox.

items.item: A stable transactional id is what lets a restarted producer recover or cleanly abort a transaction left behind by its previous instance, rather than starting over with no memory of it.

items.item: The last stable offset is the mechanism, not the guarantee — it's how a read_committed consumer knows exactly how far it's safe to read without risking a still-open transaction's eventual outcome.

items.item: Before KIP-890, one careless client that opened a transaction and never finished it could silently stall every read_committed consumer in the cluster, since the LSO can't advance past an undecided transaction.
